what_its_for: Imiglucerase is used to treat Gaucher disease, a rare inherited condition where your body does not make enough of a certain enzyme called glucocerebrosidase. Without this enzyme, fatty substances build up in your organs, bones, and bone marrow, causing problems like an enlarged spleen and liver, bone pain, anemia, and low platelet counts. This medicine replaces the missing enzyme so your body can break down these fatty substances properly.
how_to_take: Imiglucerase is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is injected slowly into a vein through a needle or catheter. It is always given by a healthcare provider in a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. You will NOT inject this medicine yourself at home unless your doctor has specifically trained you and approved home infusion. Each infusion usually takes about 1 to 2 hours. Do not rush or speed up the infusion on your own.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate your dose based on your body weight in kilograms and the severity of your disease. Doses typically range from 2.5 units per kilogram to 60 units per kilogram of body weight. Most patients receive their infusion once every 2 weeks, but your doctor may adjust the schedule based on how well you are responding to treatment. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center right away to set up a new appointment as soon as possible. Try not to go too long without your treatment, as skipping doses may allow symptoms to return or get worse. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Imiglucerase vials must be stored in a refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze the medicine. The vials are prepared and mixed by trained healthcare staff before your infusion. Once mixed, the solution should be used within 12 hours if kept at room temperature, or within 24 hours if kept refrigerated. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it.
what_to_avoid: There are no specific foods, drinks, or activities you must completely avoid while taking imiglucerase. However, always tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as interactions are possible. Avoid skipping or delaying infusion appointments. If you feel unwell before or during an infusion, tell the healthcare provider immediately rather than ignoring the symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, chest tightness, rapid or irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness or fainting, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat (signs of a serious allergic reaction), severe rash or hives, high fever, chills, severe nausea or vomiting, or unusual pain. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms of Gaucher disease, such as increased bone pain, unusual bruising or bleeding, or extreme tiredness.
when_it_works: Imiglucerase begins working right away at the cellular level, but noticeable improvements usually take time. Many patients start to feel less fatigue and see improvement in blood counts (anemia and platelet levels) within 6 months. Reductions in liver and spleen size may be seen within 6 to 12 months of regular treatment. Bone improvements may take 1 to 2 years or longer. It is very important to keep all your infusion appointments even if you do not feel immediate changes, because the medicine is still working inside your body.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. The risks and benefits of continuing imiglucerase during pregnancy should be carefully discussed with your doctor, as untreated Gaucher disease can also be harmful during pregnancy. Children: Imiglucerase can be used safely in children and is dosed based on body weight, just like in adults. Older Adults: Older patients may use this medicine; your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or Liver Problems: No specific dose adjustments are generally required, but your doctor will monitor your overall health closely. If you have a history of allergic reactions to imiglucerase or its ingredients, make sure your doctor is aware, as you may need premedication or closer monitoring during infusions.
